claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 produced by conventional melt processing exhibits multiple non-eutectic crystalline phases under both rapid and slower cooling.
The alloy exhibits a complex multistep crystallization sequence during reheating.
A high-intensity laser-quenching step immediately after conventional solidification can produce a cooling rate far above conventional rapid-cooling conditions.
Post-solidification laser quenching will kinetically suppress primary non-eutectic crystallization in this alloy.
Ultra-rapid cooling kinetically traps a disordered atomic structure.
Kinetic trapping inhibits the nucleation and growth of primary crystalline phases.
The extremely high cooling rate reduces the atomic mobility available during processing.
Reduced atomic mobility prevents formation of the critical nuclei required for primary crystallization.
Suppressing critical-nucleus formation leaves a larger fraction of the alloy amorphous.
A larger amorphous fraction enhances thermal stability during subsequent reheating.
Compared with conventional processing, laser-quenched material will exhibit fewer and smaller exothermic crystallization events during reheating.
Laser-quenched material will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than conventionally cooled material.
Conventional rapid and slower cooling produce extensive primary crystallization and a complex exothermic reheating profile in this alloy.
The intervention is beneficial only if laser quenching reaches a sufficiently high cooling rate.
The intervention is expected to remain beneficial only when controlled reheating stays below the crystallization-onset temperature.
An inadequate laser-induced cooling rate or reheating above the critical temperature may restore conventional crystallization behavior.

contradictions.description: The laser quench is specified to occur after conventional solidification, but it is claimed to prevent primary nucleation and crystallization that occur during solidification. A post-solidification quench cannot suppress crystals that have already formed unless remelting or another phase-resetting step is specified.

The stated effective boundary requires reheating to remain below crystallization onset, whereas the predicted DSC outcome and proposed experiment require heating through the onset to measure its temperature and exothermic peaks. The distinct service-heating and characterization protocols are not clarified.
